Proof. To give a non-circular proof, use the standard Dedekind-cut construction of the real numbers. A Dedekind cut is a subset A of Q satisfying: (i) A is nonempty; (ii) A is not all of Q; (iii) if p is in A and q < p, then q is in A; and (iv) A has no greatest element. In this construction, the real numbers are the Dedekind cuts, ordered by inclusion: A <= B if and only if A is a subset of B.

Let S be a nonempty set of real numbers, regarded as Dedekind cuts, and suppose that S is bounded above. Thus there is a Dedekind cut U such that A is a subset of U for every A in S. Define

L = union over A in S of A.

We first verify that L is a Dedekind cut. Because S is nonempty, choose A_0 in S. Since A_0 is nonempty and A_0 is a subset of L, the set L is nonempty. Also, every A in S is contained in U, so L is contained in U. Since U is a proper subset of Q, L is also a proper subset of Q. If p is in L and q < p, then p is in some A in S; the downward-closed property of A gives q in A, and hence q in L. Finally, if p is in L, then p is in some A in S. Since A has no greatest element, there is an r in A with p < r. Then r is in L, so L has no greatest element. Therefore L is a Dedekind cut and hence represents a real number.

For every A in S, the definition of L gives A as a subset of L. Thus A <= L for every A in S, so L is an upper bound of S. Now let V be any upper bound of S. Then A is a subset of V for every A in S. Taking the union over all A in S yields L as a subset of V, or equivalently L <= V. Hence L is less than or equal to every upper bound of S.

Consequently L is the least upper bound of S, so sup S = L exists in R. This proves the least upper bound property.
